items.title: Martin Lawrence

items.lesson: Martin Lawrence was born on April 16, 1965, in Frankfurt, Germany; he would become a pioneering comedian and actor whose work on the sitcom "Martin" and the "Bad Boys" film franchise helped establish mainstream Black comedy in the 1990s and 2000s.
items.takeaway: Tags: Filmmakers · Comedy and Comedians

items.title: Maya Angelou
items.body: On Jan 1, 1971 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Maya Angelou's poetry collection 'Just Give Me a Cool Drink of Water 'fore I Diiie' (1971) earned a Pulitzer Prize nomination, establishing her as a major voice in American poetry.
items.takeaway: Tags: Poetry · Awards

items.title: Maya Angelou
items.body: On Apr 4, 1928 in St. Louis, Missouri, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Maya Angelou was born Marguerite Annie Johnson on April 4, 1928, in St. Louis, Missouri; she would become a globally recognized poet, memoirist, and civil rights activist whose work addressed economic, racial, and sexual oppression.
items.takeaway: Tags: Authors · Poetry · Civil Rights Movements · Activist Organizations

items.title: Maya Angelou
items.body: On May 28, 2014 in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Maya Angelou died on May 28, 2014; she was a poet, memoirist, and activist whose groundbreaking work 'I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings' became transformative literature that helped survivors of sexual abuse find their voices and whose poetry collections and civil rights activism made her essential to understanding both Civil Rights-era cultural production and contemporary American letters.
items.takeaway: Tags: RIP · Poetry · Authors · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Maya Angelou
items.body: On Jan 20, 1993 in Washington, D.C., United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Maya Angelou delivered her poem 'On the Pulse of Morning' at President Bill Clinton's 1993 inauguration, becoming only the second poet in U.S. history to compose an inaugural poem; the work later won a Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album.
items.takeaway: Tags: Poetry · Authors · Awards

items.title: Maya Angelou
items.body: On Jan 1, 1960 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Maya Angelou served as northern coordinator for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference at Martin Luther King Jr.'s request and helped Malcolm X establish the Organization of Afro-American Unity, bridging creative expression and social justice activism during the Civil Rights Movement.
items.takeaway: Tags: Activist Organizations · Civil Rights Movements · Authors · Poetry

items.title: Maya Angelou
items.body: On Feb 15, 2011 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Maya Angelou received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2011, the nation's highest civilian honor, recognizing her lifetime contributions to literature and civil rights; she also earned three Grammy Awards, the National Medal of Arts (2000), and over 30 honorary degrees.
items.takeaway: Tags: Awards · Poetry · Authors · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Maya Angelou
items.body: On Jan 1, 1972 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Maya Angelou became the first African American woman to have a screenplay produced as a feature film with 'Georgia, Georgia' (1972), breaking barriers in the film industry.
items.takeaway: Tags: Famous Firsts · Authors · Poetry · Cinema and Filmmakers

items.title: Maya Angelou
items.body: On Jan 1, 1969 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Maya Angelou published 'I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings' (1969), a groundbreaking autobiographical memoir that became the first nonfiction bestseller by a Black woman and received a National Book Award nomination, establishing itself as a cornerstone of African American literature.
items.takeaway: Tags: Authors · Poetry · Awards · Women Leaders

items.title: Montrose William Thornton
items.body: On Jan 1, 1872 in Hampton, Virginia, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Rev. William Thornton served six terms as a curator of Hampton Institute beginning in 1872, contributing to an institution that trained thousands of African American teachers for the South during Reconstruction and beyond.
items.takeaway: Tags: Religious Leaders · Notable Educators

items.title: Montrose William Thornton
items.body: On Jan 1, 1815 in Hampton, Virginia, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Rev. William A. Thornton was born in 1815 in Hampton, Virginia; he would become an African American minister, community leader, and founder of Zion Baptist Church of Phoebus, where he served as pastor for 39 years and established hospitals and schools for formerly enslaved refugees.
items.takeaway: Tags: Abolition of Slavery · Abolitionists · Religious Leaders

items.title: Montrose William Thornton
items.body: On Jan 1, 1909 in Hampton, Virginia, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Rev. William A. Thornton died in 1909 in Hampton, Virginia; he was an African American minister and community leader who founded Zion Baptist Church, established hospitals and schools for formerly enslaved refugees, donated land for a cemetery, and served as a curator of Hampton Institute for six terms, leaving a legacy of religious leadership, education, and community development during Reconstruction.
items.takeaway: Tags: Abolition of Slavery · Abolitionists · Religious Leaders

items.title: Montrose William Thornton
items.body: On Jan 1, 1865 in Hampton, Virginia, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Rev. William Thornton founded the Lincoln Land Association to help formerly enslaved people purchase collective farmland, providing economic opportunities and land ownership for the freedmen community in Hampton.
items.takeaway: Tags: Abolition of Slavery · Abolitionists · Activist Organizations · Religious Leaders

items.title: Paul Robeson
items.body: On Jun 1, 1919 in New Brunswick, New Jersey, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Paul Robeson graduated as valedictorian of Rutgers University's class of 1919, where he was the school's third Black student and first Black football player, he earned 15 varsity letters across four sports, was twice named an All-American football player, and was inducted into Phi Beta Kappa.
items.takeaway: Tags: Famous Firsts · Actors and Actresses · Musicians · Activist Organizations

items.title: Paul Robeson
items.body: On Jan 23, 1976 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Paul Robeson died on January 23, 1976; he was a singer, actor, and activist who achieved worldwide acclaim for his performances in 'Show Boat' and as the first Black actor to play Othello on Broadway, while using his artistic platform to challenge systemic racism and demonstrate that artistic achievement and political activism could reinforce one another, establishing him as a symbol of resistance and dignity during the civil rights era.
items.takeaway: Tags: RIP · Actors and Actresses · Black Arts Movements

items.title: Paul Robeson
items.body: On Jan 1, 1924 in New York, New York, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Paul Robeson starred in Eugene O'Neill's 'The Emperor Jones' (1924-1925), establishing himself as a preeminent theatrical figure and breaking barriers as one of the first Black actors to achieve mainstream acclaim in American theater.
items.takeaway: Tags: Actors and Actresses · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Paul Robeson
items.body: On Apr 9, 1898 in Princeton, New Jersey, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Paul Bustill Robeson was born on April 9, 1898, in Princeton, New Jersey; he would become an acclaimed singer, actor, and political activist who achieved worldwide fame while using his artistic platform to challenge racism and connect the African American struggle for civil rights with global liberation movements.
items.takeaway: Tags: Actors and Actresses · Musicians · Activist Organizations

items.title: Paul Robeson
items.body: On Oct 19, 1943 in New York, New York, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Paul Robeson became the first Black actor to play Othello on Broadway in a 1943 production that set a record with 296 performances, the longest-running Shakespeare play on Broadway at that time.
items.takeaway: Tags: Black Arts Movements · Actors and Actresses · Musicians

items.title: Paul Robeson
items.body: On Jan 1, 1928 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Paul Robeson performed in 'Show Boat' and became world-famous for his rendition of 'Ol' Man River,' which he reinterpreted as a statement against racism and oppression, achieving international recognition through concerts and recordings in over 20 languages.
items.takeaway: Tags: Musicians · Actors and Actresses · Activist Organizations

items.title: Paul Robeson
items.body: On Jan 1, 1945 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Paul Robeson received the NAACP Spingarn Medal in 1945 for his advocacy against lynching and racial segregation, and for connecting the African American civil rights struggle with international liberation movements including antifascist causes, Welsh miners, and Indian independence.
items.takeaway: Tags: Activist Organizations · Civil Rights Movements · Awards · Actors and Actresses

items.title: Ruby Bridges
items.body: On Sep 8, 1954 in Tylertown, Mississippi, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Ruby Bridges was born on September 8, 1954, in Tylertown, Mississippi; she would become a civil rights icon as the first African American child to integrate an all-white public elementary school in the American South, demonstrating extraordinary courage that advanced school desegregation efforts.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Ruby Bridges
items.body: On Jan 1, 2005 in New Orleans, Louisiana, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, Ruby Bridges saved William Frantz Elementary School from demolition by having it placed on the National Register of Historic Places, preserving a landmark site of school desegregation history.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Ruby Bridges
items.body: On Nov 14, 1960 in New Orleans, Louisiana, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: During her first year at William Frantz Elementary, Ruby Bridges attended classes alone with teacher Barbara Henry while white parents pulled their children from the school, yet she never missed a single day despite severe harassment, objects thrown at her, and segregation from cafeterias and playgrounds.
items.takeaway: Tags: Landmark Supreme Court Cases · Women Leaders · United States · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Ruby Bridges
items.body: On Jan 1, 2000 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Ruby Bridges was named Honorary Deputy U.S. Marshal in 2000, recognizing her historic role in school desegregation and the federal marshals who protected her during her first year at William Frantz Elementary.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Civil Rights Movements · Awards

items.title: Ruby Bridges
items.body: On Nov 14, 1960 in New Orleans, Louisiana, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: On November 14, 1960, six-year-old Ruby Bridges enrolled at William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans as its only Black student, requiring federal marshal protection through hostile crowds and becoming the first African American child to integrate an all-white elementary school in the American South following the Supreme Court's Brown v. Board of Education ruling.
items.takeaway: Tags: Landmark Supreme Court Cases · Women Leaders · United States · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Ruby Bridges
items.body: On Jan 1, 1963 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Ruby Bridges' experience inspired Norman Rockwell's iconic 1963 painting 'The Problem We All Live With,' which depicts her journey to school between federal marshals and became a defining image of the civil rights movement, later displayed in the White House during President Obama's administration.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Civil Rights Movements · Landmark Supreme Court Cases

items.title: Ruby Bridges
items.body: On Jan 1, 2024 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Ruby Bridges was inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame in 2024, recognizing her transformative impact on civil rights and her decades of advocacy work promoting anti-racism education and cross-racial understanding among young people.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Ruby Bridges
items.body: On Jan 1, 1999 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Ruby Bridges established the Ruby Bridges Foundation in 1999 to promote tolerance, respect, and appreciation of all differences among schoolchildren, operating under the principle that 'Racism is a grown-up disease, and we must stop using our children to spread it.'
items.takeaway: Tags: Activist Organizations · Civil Rights Movements · Women Leaders · United States

items.title: Shirley Chisolm
items.body: On Jan 1, 1977 in Washington, D.C., United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Shirley Chisholm became the first Black woman and second woman to serve on the House Rules Committee in 1977, one of Congress's most powerful committees that determines which legislation reaches the House floor for a vote.
items.takeaway: Tags: Activist Organizations · Women Leaders · United States · Political Leaders

items.title: Shirley Chisolm
items.body: On Jan 1, 2005 in Ormond Beach, Florida, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Shirley Chisholm died on January 1, 2005; she was a pioneering politician who served seven terms in Congress (1969-1983), introduced over 50 pieces of legislation, and became the first African American woman elected to Congress and the first woman to seek the Democratic presidential nomination, leaving a legacy encapsulated in her personal motto 'Unbought and Unbossed' and posthumously receiving the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015.
items.takeaway: Tags: Activist Organizations · Civil Rights Movements · Political Leaders · United States

items.title: Shirley Chisolm
items.body: On Jan 1, 1971 in Washington, D.C., United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Shirley Chisholm co-founded the Congressional Black Caucus in 1971, establishing a coalition to strengthen the political voice of African American legislators and address issues affecting Black communities nationwide.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Political Leaders · Civil Rights Movements

items.title: Shirley Chisolm
items.body: On Jan 25, 1972 in Washington, D.C., United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Shirley Chisholm became the first woman and first African American from a major political party to seek the presidential nomination when she announced her candidacy for the 1972 Democratic nomination, entering 12 primaries and winning 152 delegate votes despite facing discrimination and limited media access.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Political Leaders

items.title: Shirley Chisolm
items.body: On Nov 30, 1924 in Brooklyn, New York, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Shirley Anita St. Hill Chisholm was born on November 30, 1924, in Brooklyn, New York; she would become a groundbreaking politician who shattered multiple barriers as the first African American woman elected to Congress and the first woman to seek the Democratic presidential nomination, championing racial equality, gender equity, and poverty reduction.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Famous Firsts

items.title: Shirley Chisolm
items.body: On Nov 5, 1968 in Brooklyn, New York, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Shirley Chisholm became the first African American woman elected to the U.S. Congress in 1968, representing Brooklyn's 12th Congressional District and defeating civil rights leader James Farmer with her campaign slogan 'Fighting Shirley Chisholm—Unbought and Unbossed.'
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Political Leaders · Famous Firsts

items.title: Shirley Chisolm
items.body: On Jul 1, 1971 in Washington, D.C., United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Shirley Chisholm co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus in 1971, creating a multipartisan organization dedicated to increasing women's participation in politics and advancing gender equity in American government.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Political Leaders

items.title: Shirley Chisolm
items.body: On Jan 1, 1974 in Washington, D.C., United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: During her congressional tenure, Shirley Chisholm secured unemployment benefits for domestic workers, established college access programs for underprivileged students, and championed the 1974 minimum wage law expansion to domestic and government workers, advancing economic justice for marginalized communities.
items.takeaway: Tags: Women Leaders · United States · Political Leaders

items.title: Tyler Perry
items.body: On Oct 1, 2019 in Atlanta, Georgia, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Tyler Perry opened a $250 million state-of-the-art Tyler Perry Studios facility in October 2019 on a former 330-acre Confederate military base in Atlanta, making it one of the largest film production studios in the United States and demonstrating Black ownership in major entertainment infrastructure.
items.takeaway: Tags: Filmmakers · Cinema and Filmmakers

items.title: Tyler Perry
items.body: On Jan 1, 2006 in Atlanta, Georgia, United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Tyler Perry established Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta in 2006, creating a vertically integrated production company that brought African American Southern entertainment to mainstream commercial platforms and later became a major production hub for films like 'Black Panther' and television series like 'The Walking Dead.'
items.takeaway: Tags: Cinema and Filmmakers · Filmmakers

items.title: Tyler Perry
items.body: On Jan 1, 2021 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Tyler Perry received the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 2021, recognized for 'caring for people who are most often ignored' and for achieving billionaire status with a net worth of approximately $1.4 billion according to Forbes, demonstrating Black excellence in entertainment ownership.
items.takeaway: Tags: Awards · Actors and Actresses · Cinema and Filmmakers

items.title: Tyler Perry
items.body: On Jan 1, 2000 in United States — a verified fact from the Black History API.
items.lesson: Tyler Perry created the iconic character Mabel 'Madea' Simmons, a gun-toting, sharp-tongued grandmother he portrays in drag, in his 2000 play 'I Can Do Bad All by Myself,' launching a franchise that would gross over $660 million and become his signature work.
items.takeaway: Tags: Cinema and Filmmakers · Filmmakers · Atlanta · Actors and Actresses
